figures.alt: The diagram shows carbon dioxide being bubbled through limewater, and the limewater turning milky / cloudy to confirm the presence of carbon dioxide
The diagram shows chloride ions forming a whilte precipitate, bromide ions forming a cream precipitate and iodide ions forming a yellow precipitate
The diagram shows barium chloride solution being added to a sample, which forms a white precipitate if sulfate ions are present

specPoints.text: describe tests for these anions: Cl–, Br– and I– using acidified silver nitrate solution; SO4 2– using acidified barium chloride solution; CO3 2– using hydrochloric acid and identifying the gas evolved

primer.text: You already know from Ionic Bonding how atoms gain or lose electrons to form ions, and that negative ions are called anions. That vocabulary is exactly what this note needs, because every test here is designed to detect one specific anion in solution. You will meet three short, parallel procedures: one for carbonate ions, one for halide ions, and one for sulfate ions, each ending in a visible positive result.

lessons.title: Test for carbonate ions
lessons.opening: Three quick tests between them identify every anion this note covers, and this lesson takes the first: the carbonate ion. A carbonate is a compound carrying CO3 2–, and acid plus limewater exposes it in seconds. The star of the test is carbon dioxide, the gas that turns limewater cloudy.
keyPoints: A carbonate compound fizzes with dilute acid because carbon dioxide gas is produced.
The test adds dilute acid, then bubbles the gas released through limewater.
Limewater turning cloudy is the positive result for the carbonate ion.
The cloudiness is a white precipitate of calcium carbonate forming in the limewater.

low.restatement: Add dilute acid to the sample, bubble the gas through limewater, and cloudiness confirms carbonate ions.
low.analogy: Think of a breathalyser for carbonates: the acid makes the suspect gas, and limewater is the strip that changes colour only for carbon dioxide.
low.examPointer: Describe the full sequence when asked: acid added, gas bubbled through limewater, limewater turns cloudy. Stating only that limewater turns cloudy names a result, not a test.

medium.restatement: The acid donates hydrogen ions to the carbonate, releasing carbon dioxide gas; that gas reacts with dissolved calcium hydroxide to deposit insoluble calcium carbonate, the white cloudiness observed.
medium.analogy: It runs like a two-stage security check: the acid questions the sample until it gives up its gas, then limewater fingerprints that gas, and only carbon dioxide produces the white cloud.
medium.examPointer: For full marks include both equations where asked: the acid-carbonate step, whose ionic form pairs CO3 2– with 2H+ to give CO2 and H2O, and the limewater step forming CaCO3.

check.stem: A gas from a carbonate sample turns limewater cloudy. Which anion was present?

options.text: Carbonate, provided the full sequence was acid added first, then the gas bubbled through limewater
options.explanation: Acid on a carbonate releases carbon dioxide, and carbon dioxide is the gas that clouds limewater.

options.text: Sulfate, because sulfates also fizz with acid
options.explanation: Sulfates do not release a gas with acid; fizzing points to carbonate.

options.text: Chloride, since limewater reacts with chlorine
options.explanation: The halide test gives silver halide precipitates, not limewater cloudiness.

options.text: Any anion, because limewater clouds for all gases
options.explanation: Limewater is specific to carbon dioxide among the gases these tests produce.

check.stem: A student writes 'limewater turns cloudy' as the complete test for carbonate ions. What is wrong with that answer?

options.text: It names only the result; the test itself, adding acid and bubbling the gas through limewater, must be described
options.explanation: The examiner wants the procedure; the cloudiness is the observation that confirms it.

options.text: Nothing; cloudiness alone is the accepted full answer
options.explanation: The exam hint is explicit that this is stating a result, not describing a test.

options.text: It should say limewater turns clear instead of cloudy
options.explanation: Cloudy is the right observation; what is missing is the procedure that produces the gas.

options.text: Limewater is the wrong reagent; universal indicator should be used
options.explanation: Limewater is the designed confirmatory reagent for carbon dioxide in this test.

check.stem: Which ionic equation represents the reaction that produces the gas in the carbonate test?

options.text: CO3 2– (aq) + 2H+ (aq) → CO2 (g) + H2O (l)
options.explanation: The carbonate ion plus two hydrogen ions gives carbon dioxide and water, the note's ionic form.

options.text: CO3 2– (aq) + H+ (aq) → CO2 (g) + H2O (l)
options.explanation: Unbalanced: one hydrogen ion cannot supply the water and balance the charge at the same time.

options.text: CO2 (g) + Ca(OH)2 (aq) → CaCO3 (s) + H2O (l)
options.explanation: That is the second step, limewater reacting with carbon dioxide, not the step that produces the gas.

options.text: CO3 2– (aq) + 2H+ (aq) → CaCO3 (s) + H2 (g)
options.explanation: No calcium is present in the acid step and hydrogen gas is not the product.

check.stem: Why does effervescence happen during the carbonate test?

options.text: Carbon dioxide gas is released as the acid reacts with the carbonate
options.explanation: Fizzing is the visible escape of the carbon dioxide the reaction produces.

options.text: The limewater boils as the gas passes through it
options.explanation: No heating is involved; the limewater stays at room temperature.

options.text: Calcium carbonate dissolves rapidly, releasing bubbles of oxygen
options.explanation: The gas is carbon dioxide, and calcium carbonate forms rather than dissolves in limewater.

options.text: The acid evaporates on contact with the sample
options.explanation: Effervescence is a reaction product escaping, not evaporation.

check.stem: In the limewater step, what is the white substance that makes the limewater cloudy?

options.text: Insoluble calcium carbonate precipitating out of the solution
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with dissolved calcium hydroxide to form solid calcium carbonate, the white cloud.

options.text: Calcium chloride, dissolved from the acid used earlier
options.explanation: Calcium chloride is soluble and colourless; it cannot cloud the limewater.

options.text: Calcium hydroxide that was already suspended in the limewater
options.explanation: Clear limewater is a true solution; the cloud appears only after carbon dioxide is added.

options.text: Calcium oxide formed when the water is consumed
options.explanation: No oxide forms in this reaction; the precipitate is the carbonate.

lessons.title: Test for halide ions
lessons.opening: The second test identifies which halide ion — chloride, bromide or iodide — a solution contains. Silver nitrate makes all three precipitate, so which ion you have comes down to the colour of the solid that appears. Just as important is the acid added first, because the wrong acid invents its own precipitate.
keyPoints: Halide ions are the negative ions formed by the Group 7 elements.
The sample is acidified with nitric acid before silver nitrate solution is added.
A precipitate of silver halide appears when a halide ion is present.
Colours identify the ion: silver chloride is white, silver bromide cream, silver iodide yellow.
Nitric acid must be used, because hydrochloric acid adds chloride ions that interfere.

low.restatement: Acidify with nitric acid, add silver nitrate solution, and read the precipitate colour: white for chloride, cream for bromide, yellow for iodide.
low.analogy: It is like three passport colours at one border desk: every halide receives a silver stamp, and only the colour tells you which ion presented itself.
low.examPointer: The acidification step must use nitric acid; hydrochloric acid would introduce chloride ions of its own and throw a white precipitate that ruins the reading.

medium.restatement: Nitric acid clears the field of ions that would react badly, then silver ions meet any halide ions present and lock into insoluble silver halides; each silver halide has its own colour, so the precipitate names the ion.
medium.analogy: Picture a darkroom tray with one developer bath and three possible print tones; the paper always darkens, but the exact shade that appears tells you which negative went in.
medium.examPointer: Quote a worded equation if asked, such as potassium chloride plus silver nitrate giving potassium nitrate plus silver chloride, and mark the silver halide product with the state symbol (s).

check.stem: Which reagent pair is used to test for halide ions?

options.text: Nitric acid to acidify, then silver nitrate solution
options.explanation: That is the note's specified sequence for the halide test.

options.text: Hydrochloric acid to acidify, then silver nitrate solution
options.explanation: HCl carries chloride ions and would create its own white precipitate.

options.text: Dilute acid, then limewater
options.explanation: That is the carbonate test's sequence, not the halide test.

options.text: Barium chloride solution alone
options.explanation: Barium chloride belongs to the sulfate test.

check.stem: A halide test gives a cream precipitate. Which ion is present?

options.text: Bromide
options.explanation: Silver bromide is the cream precipitate among the three silver halides.

options.text: Chloride
options.explanation: Silver chloride is white, not cream.

options.text: Iodide
options.explanation: Silver iodide is yellow; cream belongs to bromide.

options.text: Sulfate, because sulfates give pale colours
options.explanation: Sulfate testing relies on a white barium precipitate, not a cream one.

check.stem: Why must nitric acid, rather than hydrochloric acid, be used to acidify the sample?

options.text: Hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions, which would form a white silver chloride precipitate and spoil the result
options.explanation: The acid must not add the very ion the test is trying to detect.

options.text: Nitric acid is stronger, so the reaction finishes faster
options.explanation: Speed is irrelevant; the choice is about avoiding added chloride ions.

options.text: Hydrochloric acid would dissolve the silver halide precipitates
options.explanation: The problem is extra precipitate from the acid itself, not dissolving the real one.

options.text: Nitric acid colours the precipitates more clearly
options.explanation: The colours come from the silver halides themselves; the acid adds no colour.

check.stem: Potassium bromide solution is added to silver nitrate solution. What are the products?

options.text: Potassium nitrate solution and silver bromide precipitate
options.explanation: The ions swap partners: potassium pairs with nitrate, silver with bromide, and the silver bromide is the (s) product.

options.text: Potassium bromide and silver nitrate, unchanged
options.explanation: A precipitation reaction has occurred; the ions recombine into new substances.

options.text: Potassium silver and bromine nitrate
options.explanation: Compounds do not split into mixed-name fragments; the pairs follow the ion charges.

options.text: Silver nitrate and potassium bromide solid
options.explanation: Those are the reactants; the products are potassium nitrate and silver bromide.

check.stem: A student acidifies with HCl and gets a white precipitate after adding silver nitrate. What can they conclude?

options.text: Nothing reliable: the acid introduced chloride ions, so the white precipitate may come from the acid itself
options.explanation: The procedure was broken, so the observation cannot identify the sample's own halide.

options.text: Chloride ions were definitely in the original sample
options.explanation: The chloride may have arrived with the hydrochloric acid, not with the sample.

options.text: The sample contained bromide, since white is close to cream
options.explanation: Colour guessing does not rescue a broken procedure.

options.text: The test worked; a white precipitate always means chloride
options.explanation: A white precipitate only means chloride when the acid used was nitric acid.

lessons.title: Test for sulfate ions
lessons.opening: The final test detects the sulfate ion in solution. The pattern matches the halide test: acidify first, then add a reagent that forms an insoluble product with the target ion. Here the reagent is barium chloride, and a white precipitate of barium sulfate is the positive sign.
keyPoints: Sulfate compounds contain the sulfate ion, SO4 2–.
The sample is acidified with dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution is added.
A white precipitate of barium sulfate forms if the sulfate ion is present.
Barium nitrate solution can replace barium chloride in this test.
The hydrochloric acid removes carbonate impurities that would otherwise give a false precipitate.

low.restatement: Acidify the sample with dilute hydrochloric acid, add a few drops of barium chloride solution, and a white precipitate means sulfate ions.
low.analogy: It works like a clarifying agent dropped into muddy water: only sulfate and barium lock together into an insoluble solid, and the white settling is the confirmation.
low.examPointer: Explain why acid comes first: it removes carbonate impurities, which would otherwise form their own white precipitate and give a false positive.

medium.restatement: The acid destroys any carbonate present before the reagent goes in, so the only thing barium ions can lock onto is sulfate, precipitating insoluble barium sulfate; barium nitrate works equally well as the barium source.
medium.analogy: Think of clearing the room before the real guest arrives: the acid ushers out any carbonate gatecrashers first, so the white barium sulfate that forms can only belong to sulfate.
medium.examPointer: If a question offers barium nitrate instead of barium chloride, accept it: the barium ion is the active reagent, and swapping the acid partner changes nothing observable.

check.stem: What is the correct sequence for the sulfate ion test?

options.text: Acidify with dilute hydrochloric acid, then add a few drops of barium chloride solution
options.explanation: That matches the note's stated procedure and its order.

options.text: Add barium chloride solution first, then acidify with hydrochloric acid
options.explanation: The acid must clear carbonates before the barium reagent reveals the precipitate.

options.text: Acidify with nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution
options.explanation: That is the halide test; the sulfate test uses barium chloride.

options.text: Bubble the gas through limewater after adding acid
options.explanation: No gas is collected in the sulfate test; the signal is a precipitate in the sample.

check.stem: A white precipitate forms after acidifying and adding barium chloride. Which ion is present?

options.text: Sulfate, as insoluble barium sulfate
options.explanation: Barium ions lock onto sulfate ions to give the white barium sulfate precipitate.

options.text: Carbonate, because all carbonate salts are white
options.explanation: The acidification step destroyed any carbonates first; the surviving precipitate is the sulfate one.

options.text: Chloride, from the barium chloride reagent
options.explanation: The reagent's own ions cannot precipitate each other; barium chloride is soluble.

options.text: Barium, since barium salts are insoluble
options.explanation: Many barium salts are soluble; the precipitate is specifically barium sulfate.

check.stem: Why is hydrochloric acid added before the barium chloride solution?

options.text: To remove carbonate ions, which would otherwise form their own precipitate and interfere
options.explanation: The exam hint is explicit: carbonates left in place would produce a false precipitate.

options.text: To speed up the reaction between barium and sulfate
options.explanation: Rate is not the purpose; removing interfering ions is.

options.text: To dissolve the barium chloride more completely
options.explanation: Barium chloride already dissolves readily in water.

options.text: To neutralise any sulfate ions present
options.explanation: Neutralising sulfate would defeat the test; the acid targets carbonates.

check.stem: Barium nitrate solution is offered instead of barium chloride. What follows?

options.text: The test still works: the barium ion is the reagent that precipitates sulfate
options.explanation: The note states the test can be carried out with barium nitrate; the barium ion is the active part.

options.text: The test fails, because only barium chloride precipitates sulfate
options.explanation: It is the barium ion, not the chloride partner, that forms the precipitate.

options.text: A yellow precipitate forms instead of white
options.explanation: Barium sulfate is white whichever barium salt supplies the barium ions.

options.text: Extra acidification with nitric acid is now required
options.explanation: The acidification step stays as it is; only the barium source has changed.

check.stem: A sample is known to contain no carbonates, yet the acid step is still performed. Why is the result still trusted?

options.text: Adding the acid remains harmless: with no carbonates to remove, the white barium sulfate precipitate still identifies sulfate
options.explanation: The acid step is protective insurance; it changes nothing when no carbonate is present.

options.text: It would not be trusted: the acid destroys sulfate ions
options.explanation: Dilute hydrochloric acid does not remove sulfate ions; the precipitate still forms.

options.text: The precipitate would turn grey from the extra acid
options.explanation: Barium sulfate stays white; the acid causes no colour change.

options.text: The result doubles as a carbonate test, so two ions are confirmed
options.explanation: No gas-evolution observation is made here, so nothing about carbonate is confirmed.

glossary.definition: A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom gains electrons; the ion class all three tests here detect.
A solution of calcium hydroxide that turns cloudy in carbon dioxide; the confirming reagent of the carbonate test.
An insoluble solid that forms when two solutions react; the visible positive signal in the halide and sulfate tests.
Fizzing seen when a gas escapes a liquid; observed in the carbonate test as carbon dioxide is released.
The negative ion formed by a Group 7 element, such as chloride, bromide or iodide.
To add dilute acid to a sample before testing, removing interfering ions or releasing the gas needed.

workedExample.prompt: a) Describe the test for carbonate ions, including the ionic equation for the gas-forming step. b) Describe the test that distinguishes chloride, bromide and iodide ions, naming the three precipitate colours. c) Describe the sulfate ion test and explain why acid is added first.
steps: a) Add dilute acid to the sample — fizzing shows carbon dioxide is released — and bubble the gas through limewater, which turns cloudy if carbonate is present: CO3 2- (aq) + 2H+ (aq) → CO2 (g) + H2O (l).
b) Acidify the sample with nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution: a white precipitate shows chloride (AgCl), cream shows bromide (AgBr), and yellow shows iodide (AgI).

c) Acidify with dilute hydrochloric acid, then add barium chloride solution: a white precipitate of barium sulfate (Ba2+ (aq) + SO4 2- (aq) → BaSO4 (s)) shows sulfate ions. The acid first removes carbonate impurities, which would otherwise form their own white precipitate and give a false positive.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Acid, then limewater turns cloudy; CO3 2- + 2H+ → CO2 + H2O. b) AgNO3 after HNO3: white (Cl-), cream (Br-), yellow (I-). c) HCl then BaCl2 gives white BaSO4; the acid removes carbonate interference.
